questions.title: Two sum: return indices of two numbers that add up to target
questions.note: Hash map of value → index, one pass, O(n). Brute force O(n²) is the answer they want you to improve.

questions.title: Validate brackets: is the string balanced?
questions.note: Stack. Don't forget the final check — '((' must return False.

questions.title: Palindrome check ignoring case, spaces and punctuation
questions.given: 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama' → True
questions.note: Follow-up: O(1) space → two pointers moving inward, skipping non-alphanumeric characters.

check.args: 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'

questions.title: Second largest distinct number without sorting
questions.note: One pass, O(n). The 'a > x' check skips duplicates of the max.

questions.title: Return integers that appear more than once, sorted
questions.note: Counter is the clean answer. Same idea as finding duplicate keys before a load.

questions.title: Find the missing number in 0..n
questions.note: Sum formula, O(n) time, O(1) space. XOR of indices and values also works and avoids overflow in other languages.

questions.title: Move all zeros to the end in place, keeping order
questions.note: Two pointers, one pass, no extra list.

questions.title: Rotate a list to the right by k steps
questions.note: k %= len handles k > n. a[:] = modifies in place. In-place O(1) space version: reverse all, then reverse both parts.

questions.title: Best time to buy and sell stock (one trade)
questions.note: Track the lowest price so far. O(n). Sell must come after buy — that's why sorting is wrong.

questions.title: Forward-fill None values with the last seen value (default 0), O(1) space
questions.note: Use 'is None', not 'if not x' — that would also replace real zeros.

questions.title: Character with the longest consecutive run (earliest on ties)
questions.note: Strict > keeps the earliest character on ties.

questions.title: Return bigrams from a sentence
questions.note: zip of the list with itself shifted by one — a common one-liner trick.

questions.title: Top 3 most common words, case-insensitive, ignoring punctuation
questions.note: Lowercase first, regex to tokenize. Follow-up: drop stop-words with a set.

questions.title: Words that appear in exactly one of two sentences (case-insensitive)
questions.note: Symmetric difference ^. Know set ops: & | - ^.

questions.title: Flatten a nested dict into dot keys
questions.note: Recursion on dict values. Follow-up: very deep nesting → use an explicit stack to avoid recursion limit.

questions.title: First non-repeating character in a string, in O(n)
questions.note: Two passes, still O(n). We re-scan s, so the original order decides the answer.

questions.title: Group anagrams
questions.note: Key = sorted letters. Faster key for long words: a 26-length count tuple → O(n·k) instead of O(n·k log k).

questions.title: Merge overlapping intervals
questions.note: Sort by start, then extend or append. O(n log n). Same idea as merging overlapping time windows in pipelines.

questions.title: Top K frequent elements without sorting everything
questions.note: Heap → O(n log k) instead of O(n log n). Mention bucket sort for O(n).

questions.title: Longest substring without repeating characters
questions.note: Sliding window with last-seen index. O(n), one pass.

questions.title: Write a retry decorator with exponential backoff
questions.given: Retry an API/DB call up to 3 times: wait 1s, 2s, 4s.
questions.note: Decorator with arguments = 3 levels. In real code catch only transient errors, and add jitter.

questions.title: Count records per key in a 50 GB log file on an 8 GB machine
questions.given: Each line: 'timestamp,user_id,event'. Count events per user.
questions.answer:
from collections import Counter
def count(path):
    c = Counter()
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            c[line.split(",", 2)[1]] += 1
    return c
questions.note: Iterate line by line — never f.read(). If even the counts don't fit in memory: hash-partition users to temp files, or just use Spark.

questions.title: Implement an LRU cache with get/put in O(1)
questions.given: Capacity 2: put(1), put(2), get(1), put(3) → key 2 is evicted.
questions.note: OrderedDict = hash map + doubly linked list. Interviewer may ask you to build that list by hand.

questions.title: Trap: what does this print?
questions.given: def add(x, lst=[]): · lst.append(x) · return lst · print(add(1), add(2))
questions.answer:
# [1, 2] [1, 2]
def add(x, lst=None):
    lst = [] if lst is None else lst
    lst.append(x)
    return lst
questions.note: Default args are evaluated once at definition, so the list is shared. Both calls return the same object.

questions.title: Batch an iterator into chunks of n without loading it all
questions.note: Generator + islice → constant memory. Used for batched API calls or DB inserts.

questions.title: Rebuild a trip from shuffled (origin, destination) tickets
questions.answer:
def itinerary(pairs):
    nxt = dict(pairs)
    start = (set(nxt) - set(nxt.values())).pop()
    path = [start]
    while path[-1] in nxt:
        path.append(nxt[path[-1]])
    return path
questions.note: Start = the only origin that is never a destination. O(n).

questions.title: Pick one uniformly random element from a stream you can't store
questions.given: Stream of unknown length; one pass only.
questions.note: Reservoir sampling: keep the i-th item with probability 1/i. Generalizes to k items.

questions.title: All primes up to N efficiently
questions.note: Sieve of Eratosthenes, O(n log log n). Start crossing out at i*i.

questions.title: Fibonacci: make the naive recursive version fast
questions.note: Memoization turns O(2ⁿ) into O(n). Iterative loop with two variables = O(1) space.

questions.title: Invert a dict where many keys share the same value
questions.note: A plain {v: k} comprehension silently loses keys — that's the trap.

questions.title: Merge two sorted lists into one sorted list
questions.note: Two pointers, O(n + m). heapq.merge does this lazily for k sorted files — external sort idea.

questions.title: Kth largest element
questions.note: Min-heap of size k → O(n log k), works on a stream. Quickselect is O(n) average.

questions.title: Parse web logs: count 5xx errors per IP
questions.note: Compile the regex once outside the loop. Skip lines that don't match instead of crashing.

questions.title: Read a CSV, validate each row, separate good and bad records
questions.given: orders.csv: id, amount, order_date — some rows have text in amount or bad dates
questions.note: Quarantine bad rows, don't fail the whole load. Catch specific exceptions, not bare except.

questions.title: Deep merge two nested dicts (second one wins on conflicts)
questions.note: Real use: merging default config with environment config. Doesn't mutate the inputs.

questions.title: Write a context manager that logs how long a block takes
questions.note: try/finally so it logs even on exceptions. perf_counter, not time.time, for durations.

questions.title: Stream a large JSON-lines file and skip malformed lines
questions.note: Generator → constant memory. Log the line number so bad records can be traced.

questions.title: Trap: what does this print?
questions.given: fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)] · print([f() for f in fs])
questions.answer:
# [2, 2, 2]
fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)] # [0, 1, 2]
questions.note: Late binding: closures look up i when called, by then the loop ended at 2. Default argument captures the value.

questions.title: Trap: what does this print?
questions.answer:
# [[1, 2, 9], [3]]
import copy
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
questions.note: copy() is shallow: the inner lists are shared. deepcopy copies nested objects.

questions.title: Pandas: fill missing prices with the median price of the same category
questions.given: df(product, category, price) with NaN prices
questions.answer:
df["price"] = df.groupby("category")["price"] \
                .transform(lambda s: s.fillna(s.median()))
questions.note: transform keeps the original row shape. A global median would be wrong across categories.

questions.title: Second highest salary in each department (ties allowed)
questions.answer:
from pyspark.sql import Window as W, functions as F
w = W.partitionBy("dept").orderBy(F.desc("salary"))
df.withColumn("r", F.dense_rank().over(w)) \
  .filter("r = 2").drop("r")
questions.note: dense_rank, not row_number — ties share a rank. Follow-up: Nth highest → filter r = N.

questions.title: Keep only the latest record per key (dedup CDC data)
questions.given: orders(order_id, status, updated_at) with many versions
questions.answer:
w = W.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("updated_at"))
latest = df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)) \
           .filter("rn = 1").drop("rn")
questions.note: row_number here — exactly one row per key. dropDuplicates() can't choose WHICH row survives.

questions.title: Users who logged in 3 or more consecutive days
questions.given: logins(user_id, login_date), possibly duplicate rows per day
questions.answer:
d = df.select("user_id", "login_date").distinct()
w = W.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("login_date")
g = d.withColumn("grp",
      F.date_sub("login_date", F.row_number().over(w)))
g.groupBy("user_id", "grp").count() \
 .filter("count >= 3").select("user_id").distinct()
questions.note: Gaps-and-islands: date minus row number is constant within a streak. Distinct first, or duplicates break it.

questions.title: Running total and 7-day moving average of sales per store
questions.given: sales(store_id, sale_date, amount), one row per day
questions.answer:
w = W.partitionBy("store_id").orderBy("sale_date")
df.withColumn("running",
      F.sum("amount").over(w.rowsBetween(W.unboundedPreceding, 0))) \
  .withColumn("ma7", F.avg("amount").over(w.rowsBetween(-6, 0)))
questions.note: Missing days? rowsBetween counts rows, not days — use rangeBetween on a day number, or fill dates first.

questions.title: Sessionize clickstream: new session after 30 min of inactivity
questions.answer:
w = W.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("ts")
s = df.withColumn("gap",
      F.col("ts").cast("long") - F.lag("ts").over(w).cast("long")) \
  .withColumn("new", F.when(F.col("gap").isNull() | (F.col("gap") > 1800), 1).otherwise(0)) \
  .withColumn("session_id", F.sum("new").over(w))
questions.note: lag → flag → running sum of flags = session number. Classic pattern; also asked in SQL.

questions.title: Explode a nested JSON array and flatten the structs
questions.answer:
df.select("id", "customer.*",
          F.explode_outer("items").alias("it")) \
  .select("id", "name", "city", "it.sku", "it.qty")
questions.note: explode_outer keeps orders with empty/null items (explode drops them). struct.* flattens one level.

questions.title: SCD Type 2 load with Delta MERGE
questions.given: dim_customer(id, city, start_date, end_date, is_current); new snapshot src(id, city)
questions.answer:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
t = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "dim_customer")
cur = t.toDF().filter("is_current")
chg = src.join(cur, "id").where(src.city != cur.city).select(src["*"])
staged = chg.withColumn("mk", F.lit(None).cast("long")) \
    .unionByName(src.withColumn("mk", F.col("id")))
t.alias("t").merge(staged.alias("s"), "t.id = s.mk AND t.is_current") \
 .whenMatchedUpdate(condition="t.city <> s.city",
     set={"is_current": "false", "end_date": "current_date()"}) \
 .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={"id": "s.id", "city": "s.city", "start_date": "current_date()",
             "end_date": "null", "is_current": "true"}).execute()
questions.note: Trick: changed rows appear twice — once with a merge key (to close the old row), once with NULL key (to insert the new one). Explain the idea; exact syntax is less important.

questions.title: Fix a skewed join with salting
questions.given: big(customer_id, ...) where a few customers have most rows; small dim(customer_id, ...)
questions.answer:
N = 10
big_s = big.withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * N).cast("int"))
dim_s = dim.withColumn("salt", F.explode(F.sequence(F.lit(0), F.lit(N - 1))))
out = big_s.join(dim_s, ["customer_id", "salt"]).drop("salt")
questions.note: Try first: broadcast(dim) if small, or AQE spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled. Salt only hot keys in practice.

questions.title: Customers who bought product A but never product B
questions.answer:
a = df.filter("product = 'A'").select("customer_id").distinct()
b = df.filter("product = 'B'").select("customer_id")
a.join(b, "customer_id", "left_anti")
questions.note: left_anti = NOT EXISTS. Cheaper and null-safe compared to NOT IN.

questions.title: Count nulls in every column in one pass
questions.answer:
df.select([F.sum(F.col(c).isNull().cast("int")).alias(c)
           for c in df.columns])
questions.note: One select = one job. A Python loop of df.filter(...).count() per column = 100 jobs.

questions.title: Why is this slow, and how do you fix it?
questions.given: for c in cols: df = df.withColumn(c, F.trim(c)) # 300 columns
questions.answer:
df = df.select([F.trim(c).alias(c) if c in cols else c
                for c in df.columns])
questions.note: Each withColumn adds a projection; hundreds of them bloat the plan and slow analysis. One select (or withColumns in Spark 3.3+).

questions.title: Pivot monthly sales: one row per product, a column per month
questions.answer:
months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]
df.groupBy("product").pivot("month", months).sum("amount").fillna(0)
questions.note: Passing the value list skips an extra job to find distinct months and fixes column order.

questions.title: Word count with the DataFrame API
questions.answer:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
df.select(F.explode(F.split(F.lower("line"), r"\W+")).alias("w")) \
  .filter("w != ''") \
  .groupBy("w").count().orderBy(F.desc("count"))
questions.note: split + explode = one row per word. RDD version uses reduceByKey, never groupByKey (shuffles everything).

questions.title: Count events per user, including users with zero events
questions.answer:
users.join(activity, "user_id", "left") \
     .groupBy("user_id", "name") \
     .agg(F.count("event_id").alias("events"))
questions.note: Left join keeps inactive users. count(column) ignores nulls → 0; count('*') would wrongly give 1.

questions.title: Read a file delimited by '~|'
questions.answer:
df = spark.read.option("header", True) \
          .option("sep", "~|").csv(path)
questions.note: Spark 3+ supports multi-character separators. On Spark 2: read as text and split.

questions.title: Load a file that has corrupt records without failing the job
questions.given: JSON/CSV where some rows are malformed
questions.answer:
df = spark.read.schema(schema_with_corrupt_col) \
     .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE") \
     .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_corrupt_record") \
     .json(path).cache()
bad = df.filter("_corrupt_record IS NOT NULL")
good = df.filter("_corrupt_record IS NULL").drop("_corrupt_record")
questions.note: Modes: PERMISSIVE / DROPMALFORMED / FAILFAST. Cache before filtering on the corrupt column. Databricks: badRecordsPath.

questions.title: Combine two files with different schemas
questions.answer: out = df1.unionByName(df2, allowMissingColumns=True)
questions.note: union() matches by POSITION and silently mixes columns. unionByName matches by name; missing columns become null.

questions.title: Top 3 products by revenue in each category
questions.answer:
rev = df.groupBy("category", "product").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("rev"))
w = W.partitionBy("category").orderBy(F.desc("rev"))
rev.withColumn("r", F.dense_rank().over(w)).filter("r <= 3")
questions.note: Aggregate first, then rank. Say whether ties should be included (dense_rank) or not (row_number).

questions.title: Employees who earn more than their manager
questions.answer:
e, m = df.alias("e"), df.alias("m")
e.join(m, F.col("e.manager_id") == F.col("m.id")) \
 .filter("e.salary > m.salary").select("e.name")
questions.note: Self join with aliases — otherwise column names are ambiguous.

questions.title: Employees earning above their department average
questions.answer:
w = W.partitionBy("dept")
df.withColumn("dept_avg", F.avg("salary").over(w)) \
  .filter("salary > dept_avg")
questions.note: Window aggregate keeps every row — no groupBy + join back needed.

questions.title: Month-over-month revenue growth %
questions.answer:
m = df.groupBy(F.trunc("order_date", "month").alias("month")) \
      .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("rev"))
w = W.orderBy("month")
m.withColumn("prev", F.lag("rev").over(w)) \
 .withColumn("growth_pct", F.round((F.col("rev") - F.col("prev")) / F.col("prev") * 100, 2))
questions.note: Window without partitionBy moves all rows to one partition — fine here only because monthly data is tiny.

questions.title: New vs returning customers per month
questions.answer:
o = df.withColumn("month", F.trunc("order_date", "month"))
first = o.groupBy("customer_id").agg(F.min("month").alias("first_month"))
o.join(first, "customer_id") \
 .withColumn("type", F.when(F.col("month") == F.col("first_month"),
"new").otherwise("returning")) \
 .groupBy("month", "type").agg(F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("customers"))
questions.note: First-purchase month per customer is the key idea. Very common in e-commerce rounds.

questions.title: Fill missing dates per store with 0 sales
questions.given: sales(store_id, d, amount) — some days missing
questions.answer:
b = df.groupBy("store_id").agg(F.min("d").alias("s"), F.max("d").alias("e"))
cal = b.select("store_id",
        F.explode(F.sequence("s", "e", F.expr("interval 1 day"))).alias("d"))
cal.join(df, ["store_id", "d"], "left").fillna(0, ["amount"])
questions.note: Build a calendar with sequence + explode, then left join. Needed before moving averages.

questions.title: Forward-fill nulls with the last known value per device
questions.given: readings(device_id, ts, temp) — temp sometimes null
questions.answer:
w = W.partitionBy("device_id").orderBy("ts") \
     .rowsBetween(W.unboundedPreceding, 0)
df.withColumn("temp_filled", F.last("temp", ignorenulls=True).over(w))
questions.note: last(..., ignorenulls=True) over a growing window. Backward fill: first(..., True) with rowsBetween(0, unboundedFollowing).

questions.title: Split full name into first and last name
questions.answer:
s = F.split("full_name", " ", 2)
df.withColumn("first", s[0]).withColumn("last", s[1])
questions.note: The limit argument (Spark 3+) keeps the rest of the name together.

questions.title: Comma-separated tags to rows, and back to an ordered list
questions.answer:
rows = df.select("id", F.explode(F.split("tags", ",")).alias("tag"))
back = rows.groupBy("id").agg(F.sort_array(F.collect_list("tag")).alias("tags"))
questions.note: collect_list order is NOT guaranteed after a shuffle — sort it, or collect structs with a timestamp and sort.

questions.title: Find fully duplicate rows and how many times each appears
questions.answer: df.groupBy(df.columns).count().filter("count > 1")
questions.note: To remove: dropDuplicates(). To remove by key: dropDuplicates(['id']) — but it keeps an arbitrary row.

questions.title: Compare yesterday's and today's snapshot: inserted, deleted, updated rows
questions.answer:
cols = [c for c in new.columns if c != "id"]
h = lambda d: d.withColumn("h", F.sha2(F.concat_ws("||",
        *[F.coalesce(F.col(c).cast("string"), F.lit("~")) for c in cols]), 256))
j = h(old).alias("o").join(h(new).alias("n"), "id", "full")
j.withColumn("status",
    F.when(F.col("o.h").isNull(), "inserted")
     .when(F.col("n.h").isNull(), "deleted")
     .when(F.col("o.h") != F.col("n.h"), "updated"))
questions.note: Row hash = one comparison instead of N columns. coalesce nulls first — concat_ws silently skips them.

questions.title: Upsert (SCD Type 1) into a Delta table
questions.answer:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
t = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "target")
t.alias("t").merge(upd.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id") \
 .whenMatchedUpdateAll() \
 .whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()
questions.note: Dedup the source first — MERGE fails if multiple source rows match one target row.

questions.title: Incremental load: only pick rows changed since the last run
questions.given: src(id, ..., updated_at), target table already loaded
questions.answer:
last = spark.table("target").agg(F.max("updated_at")).first()[0]
inc = src if last is None else src.filter(F.col("updated_at") > F.lit(last))
# then MERGE inc into target
questions.note: Handle the first run (None). Safer in prod: store the watermark in a control table, and use a small overlap + MERGE for late rows.

questions.title: Parse a JSON string column into columns
questions.answer:
schema = "id INT, items ARRAY<STRUCT<sku: STRING, qty: INT>>"
df.withColumn("j", F.from_json("payload", schema)) \
  .select("j.id", F.explode("j.items").alias("it")) \
  .select("id", "it.sku", "it.qty")
questions.note: Always give an explicit schema — inference scans the data and drifts. schema_of_json helps you draft it.

questions.title: A daily job writes 2,000 tiny files. Fix it
questions.answer:
df.repartition("dt").write.partitionBy("dt").parquet(path)
# or fewer files without full shuffle:
df.coalesce(8).write.parquet(path)
questions.note: repartition by the partition column → ~1 file per partition. coalesce avoids a shuffle but can create uneven files. Delta: OPTIMIZE / auto-compaction.

questions.title: Join a 2 TB fact table with a 50 MB dimension table efficiently
questions.answer: out = fact.join(F.broadcast(dim), "customer_id")
questions.note: Broadcast avoids shuffling 2 TB. Default auto threshold is 10 MB (spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold). Never broadcast a big table — driver OOM.

questions.title: Rewrite this Python UDF with native functions
questions.given: def tier(a): return 'high' if a >= 1000 else 'mid' if a >= 100 else 'low'
questions.answer:
df.withColumn("tier",
    F.when(F.col("amount") >= 1000, "high")
     .when(F.col("amount") >= 100, "mid")
     .otherwise("low"))
questions.note: Python UDFs serialize every row to a Python worker and block optimizations. Native when/otherwise runs in the JVM — often several times faster.

questions.title: When you must use Python logic, write a vectorized UDF
questions.given: Clean a text column with pandas string methods
questions.note: pandas_udf uses Arrow and processes batches, much faster than row-by-row udf. Still prefer native functions first.

questions.title: Kafka is at-least-once. Deduplicate events in a stream
questions.answer:
deduped = stream.withWatermark("event_ts", "10 minutes") \
                .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"])
questions.note: Watermark bounds the state. Spark 3.5+; on older versions use dropDuplicates(['event_id', 'event_ts']) with a watermark. Sink should also be idempotent (MERGE).

questions.title: Count page views per 10-minute window in a stream, allowing 15 minutes of late
questions.answer:
agg = clicks.withWatermark("ts", "15 minutes") \
            .groupBy(F.window("ts", "10 minutes"), "page").count()
agg.writeStream.outputMode("append").format("delta") \
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/pv").start("/delta/pv")
questions.note: Append mode emits a window only after the watermark passes it. Events later than 15 min are dropped.

questions.title: Median salary per department
questions.answer: df.groupBy("dept").agg(F.percentile_approx("salary", 0.5).alias("median"))
questions.note: Exact median is expensive at scale; percentile_approx is the standard answer. Spark 3.4+ also has F.median.

questions.title: Customers with no orders in the last 90 days
questions.answer:
recent = orders.filter(F.col("order_date") >= F.date_sub(F.current_date(), 90)) \
              .select("customer_id")
customers.join(recent, "customer_id", "left_anti")
questions.note: left_anti = 'not in the other table'. Churn-type question, very common.

questions.title: Find missing IDs in a sequence
questions.answer:
lo, hi = df.agg(F.min("id"), F.max("id")).first()
spark.range(lo, hi + 1).join(df, "id", "left_anti")
questions.note: spark.range builds the full sequence (column named id). Alternative: lead(id) - id > 1 to find gap ranges.
